title: Event Connections
summary: Events are broadcast lists: Connect registers your function, and EVERY registered handler runs whenever the event fires — unless you Disconnect. Connections are objects you own: keep them, disconnect them, don't leak them.

explanation.whatItIs: A connection is a live wire between an event and your function. Events don't care how many wires attach — they energize all of them, in registration order.
explanation.whyItExists: Many systems care about the same moment (a touch, a player joining); broadcasting lets each subscribe independently.
whenToUse: Connect for persistent reactions; store the returned connection
Disconnect when the reaction should stop (object death, round end)
Wait() in a thread for sequencing on the next fire
whenNotToUse: Connecting repeatedly per frame/per spawn without disconnecting — duplicate handlers stack
explanation.mentalModel:
```text
Touched
  ├─ wire 1 → handler A
  ├─ wire 2 → handler B   ← fire: A runs, THEN B
  └─ wire 3 → handler C

Disconnect = pull ONE wire.
Leak = wires you forgot you plugged in.
```
tips: Once covers 90% of one-shot needs — no manual cleanup
Guard re-entrancy: handlers can fire overlapping (multiple touches same frame)
Connection objects also expose .Connected to check
commonMistakes: Re-Connecting in a loop: N handlers doing the job N times
Never disconnecting handlers on destroyed/short-lived objects
Assuming handler order across different scripts — only registration order within a script is predictable

examples.title: Connect vs Once vs Wait
examples.code:
local prompt = workspace.Part.ProximityPrompt

-- Persistent:
local conn = prompt.Triggered:Connect(function(player)
    print(player.Name, "triggered")
end)
-- later: conn:Disconnect()

-- One-shot, auto-cleaning:
workspace.Treasure.Touched:Once(function(hit)
    print("First touch only:", hit.Name)
end)

-- Sequencing:
task.spawn(function()
    prompt.Triggered:Wait()
    print("Someone triggered it — continuing!")
end)
